d: Learn how to manage and optimize your place files in Roblox.
h:
import PlaceSizeLimit from '../includes/place-size-limit.md'

Each Roblox game consists of one or more places, and Studio uploads your place data to Roblox's servers whenever you save or publish to Roblox in the File menu.

You might also want to export local copies of places for use with a version control system or other external tools. To export your place in Studio, select Save to File or Download a Copy from the File menu. Studio offers two file formats:

  • .rbxl is the binary place file format. This format is compact, but not human-readable.
  • .rbxlx is the XML-based place file format, which is quite a bit larger on disk than the binary format.

Auto-recovery files

If saving to Roblox fails due to the file size limit, Studio automatically generates a backup of your place called a recovery file. The frequency of auto-recovery backups depends on whether your game has collaboration enabled:

  • If you have collaboration enabled and saving to Roblox fails, Studio backs up the last three save attempts as recovery files on your system.
  • If collaboration is disabled, Studio uses Auto-Recovery settings from Studio Settings.

On Windows, recovery files are located in C:\Users\Admin\AppData\Local\Roblox\RobloxStudio\AutoSaves.

On Mac, you can find them in /Users/your-username/Library/Application Support/Roblox/RobloxStudio/AutoSaves/.

Troubleshoot place file size

If you reach the 100 MB limit on your place file, there's likely an underlying issue that you can troubleshoot. Try the following steps.

Safety check

Check the models in your place and their attached scripts for any obfuscated or unclear text. This text does not compress well and might even be a malicious backdoor into your place. Roblox moderation systems actively filter out these models, but if you happen to find one, delete the model from your place, find the model on the Creator Store, and report it immediately.

Redundant parts

Unreferenced or hidden assets can accumulate over time and unnecessarily increase file size.

  1. See if any models or groups of parts are taking up more space than others:

  2. Export your place file and note its size on disk.

  3. Open the file in Roblox Studio.
  4. Copy and paste the models or groups of parts that you suspect are inordinately large.

  5. Save the file again and note its increase in file size.

  6. Check for redundant parts (parts of the same size and shape with the same position) or instances (redundant SurfaceAppearances, textures, etc.) and delete them. The Creator Store has plugins that can help you identify these cases.

Simplify terrain

Reducing or simplifying terrain can significantly reduce place size and improve performance. Avoiding excessive terrain features like dense forests or complex hills helps make games run faster and more efficiently. Of course, the game should match your artistic vision, but consider the following optimizations:

  1. Horizontal layers of the same material/occupancy compress much better than sloped layers. If possible, try to limit subsurface detail to horizontal layers.
  2. Turn on Show Wireframe Rendering from Studio's View menu and check for messy holes or misplaced water under the terrain surface. These mistakes can increase compressed size.
  3. There are community plugins that optimize non-visible blocks of terrain for better compression, such as this one.

Collision fidelity

Box and Hull collision fidelity are more memory efficient than the default. Select your meshes, open the Properties window, and change the CollisionFidelity values as appropriate for your use case.

Teleports

If other size reduction strategies fail, you can break your place into multiple, smaller places and link them through teleports. Serialization and upload happen at the place level, so this approach lets you grow your universe place by place over time instead of trying to maintain a single, massive place.

kid.simple: A place file is the saved copy of one place in your game. Studio saves it to Roblox's servers when you save or publish, but you can also download a copy to your computer. This page explains the two file types, where Studio keeps backup files if saving fails, and what to do if your place gets too big (over 100 MB). Big places save slowly and can even stop saving, so it is good to know how to slim them down.
kid.analogy: A place file is like a packed suitcase for your level. If it gets too heavy, the airline will not take it, so you look for doubled-up clothes, fold things flatter, or split your stuff into two suitcases.
keyPoints: Each place is saved to Roblox when you use Save or Publish in the File menu.
To keep a copy on your computer, use File > Save to File or Download a Copy.
`.rbxl` files are small binary files you cannot read as text. `.rbxlx` files are XML text files that are much larger.
If saving fails because the place is too big, Studio makes recovery files (backups) in an AutoSaves folder on your computer.
Check models from the Creator Store for scrambled, unreadable script text. It can be a backdoor that lets someone control your game, so delete and report it.
Look for doubled parts in the same spot and extra unused textures or SurfaceAppearances, and delete them.
Keep terrain simple, prefer flat horizontal layers underground, and fix hidden holes or stray water.
Setting mesh CollisionFidelity to Box or Hull uses less memory. If all else fails, split one huge place into several places joined by teleports.

terms.place file: The saved data for one place: every part, script, and setting in it.
terms.binary: Stored as computer-only data (ones and zeros), not readable text. It takes less space.
terms.XML: A text format with tags, like `<Part>`. You can read it, but it takes more space.
terms.version control system: A tool such as Git that keeps track of every change to your files so you can go back or compare.
terms.recovery file: An automatic backup Studio makes so you do not lose work if a save fails. With collaboration on, it keeps the last 3 failed save attempts.
terms.obfuscated: Code scrambled on purpose so people cannot read it. In free models it often hides something sneaky.
terms.backdoor: Hidden code that lets someone else secretly control or change your game.
terms.redundant: Extra and not needed. Two identical parts in the exact same spot means one is redundant.
terms.compress: Squeeze data so it takes less space. Simple repeating things, like flat terrain layers, squeeze well.
terms.collision fidelity: How exactly the game matches a mesh's real shape when things bump into it. `Box` uses a simple box around it, `Hull` a tight wrapper shape, and both save memory compared to the default.
terms.teleport: Sending players from one place to another place in the same game.
terms.serialization: Turning the objects in your place into a file so it can be saved or uploaded.

watchOut: Adding lots of free models without checking their scripts. Some contain hidden backdoors and also bloat your file. Look inside before you keep them.
Panicking when a save fails. Check the AutoSaves folder for your recovery file before redoing work.
Filling the underground with detailed, sloped terrain nobody will see. It makes the file much larger for no benefit.
